passages.t: The LORD made David victorious wherever he went
passages.happening:
David defeats the Philistines and takes Gath and its villages (verse 1). The Moabites become subject to him and bring tribute (verse 2). He defeats Hadadezer king of Zobah, ‘who had marched out to establish his dominion along the Euphrates River’ (verse 3), keeps only a hundred of his chariot horses and disables the rest (verse 4), and defeats the Arameans of Damascus who come to help him (verse 5). ‘So the LORD made David victorious wherever he went’ (verse 6).

David brings Hadadezer's gold shields to Jerusalem and takes a large amount of bronze from his cities, ‘with which Solomon made the bronze Sea, the pillars, and various bronze articles’ (verse 8). King Tou of Hamath sends his son with gifts, and David dedicates them to the LORD with the silver and gold from all the nations he has subdued (verses 9-11). Abishai defeats the Edomites in the Valley of Salt, and Edom too is subject to David. ‘So the LORD made David victorious wherever he went’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
In chapter 17 God promised, ‘I will subdue all your enemies’ (17:10). This chapter shows the promise kept, and the refrain twice says who did it. The report moves round the compass: west to the Philistines, east to Moab, north to Zobah, Damascus and Hamath, south to Edom. The word for made victorious, yasha, is the root of the words for salvation and of the names Joshua and Jesus. In battle it means to give victory, and the chapter gives it to God.

This was the high point of Israel's power, in about the early tenth century BC. At that time neither Egypt nor Assyria was pressing into the region, which helps explain how a kingdom in the hills of Judah could dominate its neighbors. Zobah was an Aramean kingdom north of Damascus; Hamath lay farther north on the Orontes River. Tribute was the regular payment a weaker kingdom made to a stronger one in return for peace, and garrisons enforced it. Disabling chariot horses took them out of war, as Joshua had done, and the law warned Israel's kings against gathering many horses. Dedicating spoil to the LORD set it apart for the sanctuary rather than the king's treasury.

The Chronicler follows 2 Samuel 8 closely but not mechanically. Some numbers and names differ, as copied numbers and place names often did: where verse 4 has seven thousand charioteers, the Hebrew of 2 Samuel 8:4 has seventeen hundred horsemen, and the cities Tibhath and Cun appear as Betah and Berothai in 2 Samuel 8:8. He leaves out how the Moabite prisoners were treated in 2 Samuel 8:2. He credits the Edomite victory to Abishai, where 2 Samuel 8:13 names David and the heading of Psalm 60 names Joab; a commander's victory was also counted as the king's. And he looks ahead: the bronze becomes the temple's bronze, and the dedicated treasure prepares for chapter 22, where David gathers materials for the house his son will build.
passages.later: The law for kings said, ‘But the king must not acquire many horses for himself or send the people back to Egypt to acquire more horses’ (Deuteronomy 17:16). A psalm of David says, ‘Some trust in chariots and others in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God’ (Psalm 20:7).
passages.asks: The chapter twice says that the LORD gave the victory. Ask which of your successes you have quietly credited to yourself. And ask what you have taken from your victories and set apart for God.

passages.t: Justice and righteousness, and the king's officials
passages.happening: ‘Thus David reigned over all Israel and administered justice and righteousness for all his people’ (verse 14). Joab is over the army, Jehoshaphat is the recorder, Zadok and Ahimelech are priests, Shavsha is the scribe, Benaiah is over the Cherethites and Pelethites, ‘and David’s sons were chief officials at the king’s side’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Verse 14 is the hinge of the chapter. After the list of conquests, David's power is summed up not by territory but by just rule. Justice, mishpat, in a king's hands means judging cases fairly and setting things right. Righteousness, tsedaqah, is conduct that fits a right relationship and keeps its obligations. Together they are the Old Testament's standard summary of good kingship: rule that protects the weak and upholds right order.

A war report followed by a list of officials was a standard form in royal records. The recorder kept official records or served as herald. The Cherethites and Pelethites are usually understood as a royal bodyguard of foreign origin, their names commonly linked with Crete and with the Philistines.

Where 2 Samuel 8:18 says David's sons were priests, the Hebrew word kohanim, Chronicles calls them chief officials at the king's side. Many think the Chronicler did this to avoid confusion with the priests descended from Aaron, in a book where priestly lines matter a great deal.
passages.later: Isaiah promised a son of David whose reign would be ‘to establish and sustain it with justice and righteousness from that time and forevermore’ (Isaiah 9:7).
passages.asks: David's power was measured by justice and righteousness for all his people. Ask how the power you hold, at home, at work or in a church, is used for those under it. And ask who would be protected if you ruled your small part of the world this way.
